candidates.quote: Begin here. It is raining. I look out on the maple, where a few leaves have turned yellow, and listen to Punch, the parrot, talking to himself and to the rain ticking gently against the windows.
candidates.author: May Sarton
candidates.locator: the first entry, September 15th (W. W. Norton, 1973)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It hands the reader the first minute of a quiet day and asks nothing of it: rain on the window, one yellow leaf, and permission to begin.

candidates.quote: Every landscape is, as it were, a state of the soul, and whoever penetrates into both is astonished to find how much likeness there is in each detail.
candidates.author: Henri-Frédéric Amiel
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written on an October walk in the rain, it tells the reader that what is outside the window and what is inside them are the same weather.

candidates.quote: There was no one waterfall above another—it was a sound of waters in the air—the voice of the air.
candidates.author: Dorothy Wordsworth
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two people lying still with their eyes shut until the separate waterfalls resolve into one sound: the whole practice of the month in a single clause.

candidates.quote: In autumn the evenings, when the glittering sun sinks close to the edge of the hills and the crows fly back to their nests in threes and fours and twos; more charming still is a file of wild geese, like specks in the distant sky.
candidates.author: Sei Shōnagon
candidates.locator: section 1, the autumn sentence of the opening list
candidates.whyThisMonth: A thousand years old and still the best instruction for looking out of a window in October: watch the light go, and count the birds.

candidates.quote: A very strange and solemn feeling came over me as I stood there, with no sound but the rustle of the pines, no one near me, and the sun so glorious, as for me alone.
candidates.author: Louisa May Alcott
candidates.locator: ch. III, Fruitlands, the entry headed Concord, Thursday (ed. Ednah D. Cheney, 1889)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A girl alone in the autumn woods before the dew is off the grass, which is close to where the reader is standing at six.

candidates.quote: When I pass the apple stalls I cannot help stopping and staring until I feel that I, myself, am changing into an apple, too—and that at any moment I may produce an apple, miraculously, out of my own being like the conjurer produces the egg.
candidates.author: Katherine Mansfield
candidates.locator: letter to Dorothy Brett, 11 October 1917 (ed. O’Sullivan and Scott, 1984)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Attention taken to its limit, where looking hard enough at an apple begins to turn you into one: the argument of the month, made cheerful.

candidates.quote: Be regular and orderly in your life, like a bourgeois, so that you may be violent and original in your work.
candidates.author: Gustave Flaubert
candidates.whyThisMonth: For anyone who suspects that an orderly, uneventful morning is a waste, here is the case that the quiet is where the work comes from.

candidates.quote: But to look at the stars always makes me dream, as simply as I dream over the black dots of a map representing towns and villages.
candidates.author: Vincent van Gogh
candidates.locator: letter 506 to Theo, Arles, about 9 July 1888
candidates.whyThisMonth: Looking up and letting the mind go, with nothing asked of the looking: a wondering line rather than a grieving one.

candidates.quote: What one seems to want in art, in experiencing it, is the same thing that is necessary for its creation, a self-forgetful, perfectly useless concentration.
candidates.author: Elizabeth Bishop
candidates.locator: 8 January 1964, in Poems, Prose, and Letters (Library of America, 2008)
candidates.whyThisMonth: It gives the reader a name for what an early hour is actually for: a self-forgetful, perfectly useless concentration.

candidates.quote: Meanwhile, let us have a sip of tea. The afternoon glow is brightening the bamboos, the fountains are bubbling with delight, the soughing of the pines is heard in our kettle. Let us dream of evanescence and linger in the beautiful foolishness of things.
candidates.author: Okakura Kakuzō
candidates.locator: chapter I, The Cup of Humanity, the closing words (1906)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The warmest invitation in the language to stop, drink something hot, and let the day be small for a moment.

candidates.quote: What a strange, demented feeling it gives me when I realize I have spent whole days before this inkstone, with nothing better to do, jotting down at random whatever nonsensical thoughts have entered my head.
candidates.author: Yoshida Kenkō
candidates.locator: the prefatory passage, the opening sentence (Columbia, 1967)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The patron saint of idle mornings admits he has spent whole days writing down nothing much, and the admission is the gift.

candidates.quote: I should say: the house shelters day-dreaming, the house protects the dreamer, the house allows one to dream in peace.
candidates.author: Gaston Bachelard
candidates.locator: chapter 1, The House. From Cellar to Garret
candidates.whyThisMonth: A sentence about the room the reader is sitting in, and why it is the right place to be doing nothing in particular.

candidates.quote: In the highlands you woke up in the morning and thought: Here I am, where I ought to be.
candidates.author: Isak Dinesen
candidates.locator: Book One, The Ngong Farm, chapter 1 (Putnam, 1937)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Waking and knowing you are where you should be is the quietest happiness there is, and she puts it in one breath.

candidates.quote: At any rate, that is happiness; to be dissolved into something complete and great.
candidates.author: Willa Cather
candidates.locator: Book I, The Shimerdas, chapter II, the closing words (1918)
candidates.speaker: Jim Burden
candidates.whyThisMonth: Lying in the sun wanting to be nothing more: the purest description of rest in the month, and the line Cather chose to be remembered by.

candidates.quote: Above all, he learned from it how to listen, to listen with a still heart, with a waiting, open soul, without passion, without desire, without judgment, without opinions.
candidates.author: Hermann Hesse
candidates.whyThisMonth: It turns listening into a discipline with a method: a still heart, a waiting soul, and no opinions yet this early.

candidates.quote: There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.
candidates.author: Charlotte Brontë
candidates.locator: chapter 1, the opening sentence (Smith, Elder and Co., 1847)
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most famous sentence in English about a day you cannot go out, which is an invitation to stay in and be still.
